hint: Ask what a board member could not possibly know from the draft as written: who changes what, for how long, and what result would count as failure.
title: Rescue a vague school-start claim

fields.label: Your verdicts on all three checklist questions, your rewritten claim, and the point that still needs evidence
criteria: Gives an explicit verdict for each of the three questions rather than a general impression
Grounds each verdict in specific words of the draft, such as 'should start later' or 'everyone knows'
Rewritten claim names concrete scope: who makes what change, for what trial period, and how it will be judged
Rewritten claim implies a test whose failure condition is stated or clearly derivable, with no invented statistics or studies
Stays on the school-start-time subject and separates what the draft asserts from what would need real evidence

instructions:
Original fictional draft. A student writes to the school board: "Our school should start later because tired students cannot learn, and everyone knows mornings are hard."

Your task, in one response: first run the three checklist questions on this draft — is it disputable (could a reasonable critic reject it?), does it have concrete scope (does a reader know exactly who changes what, and how the decision will be judged?), and does it imply a test (is there a check that could fail)? Give a verdict of pass or needs work for each question, with reasons drawn from the draft's own wording. Then rewrite the claim so it passes all three questions. Keep the school-start-time subject; do not invent statistics, studies, or survey numbers — the rewrite may set conditions and comparisons (for example, a trial period, and something to measure against something else) but no fabricated evidence. Finally, note one thing the original draft asserts that would still need real evidence to support it.

steps.explanation: A strong response runs the checklist on the draft's own words. Disputable: pass — a critic could argue that a later start shortens after-school activities or that parents' schedules depend on the current time, so the draft takes a side someone could reject. Concrete scope: needs work — 'should start later' names no school-wide change, no trial period, and no basis for judging success; 'everyone knows mornings are hard' is an appeal to common feeling, not a scope. Implies a test: needs work — nothing in the draft could fail; no measurement or comparison is proposed. A model rewrite: 'Our school should shift its first bell later for one term and then compare student attendance and reported alertness in first-period classes against a normal term before deciding whether to keep the change.' It names who (the school), what (shifting the first bell), a trial period (one term), and an evaluation (attendance and alertness compared with a normal term); if attendance and alertness do not improve, the case for the change collapses, so the test can fail. Note that the rewrite invents no numbers — the comparisons are conditions, not fabricated results. One point still needing evidence: 'tired students cannot learn' is an assertion; supporting it would require real attendance records or a sourced study, which the learner should name as a gap rather than fill.
